title: Truthful witness
hookLine: no false witness: gossip, spin, half-truths

cards: A sentence drifts across a lunch table: she's not really sick, you know. Nobody swore an oath. Nothing in it is quite a lie.
And by evening a few people see her a little differently. Some readers hear a courtroom behind today's commandment, a place where one witness could ruin a neighbor's life.
The King James Bible gives it like this: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour."
But Christian teachers have carried it out of the courtroom and into every room where one person describes another who isn't there to answer. The lunch table counts.

teach.b: Start with how Proverbs describes gossip: "The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly." Gossip isn't loud, but the wound goes deep.

Proverbs also lists a false witness that speaketh lies among the things the Lord hates, right beside the one who sows discord among brothers. So a lie about someone is never just a private slip. It splits people apart.

Now the harder part: what if the thing you say is true? The Catholic catechism names a sin called detraction: making known someone's real faults to people who had no need to know, without good reason. The fact is true.
The harm is real anyway. Martin Luther, in his Small Catechism, turns the commandment around. It isn't only don't lie about your neighbor.
It's defend your neighbor, speak well of them, and put the kindest reading on what they do. Spin and half-truths fail that test, even when every word could be checked.
Paul gives the reason underneath it all, in his letter to the Ephesians: "speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another."
In Paul's picture, a lie about one member of the body is a lie told to the whole body. A truthful witness, then, is more than someone who avoids lies.
It's someone a neighbor would be glad to have in the room when they aren't.

how: Some Christians learn this commandment in catechism classes and examine their speech by it before confession or in personal prayer; Luther's Small Catechism and the Catholic catechism both apply it to gossip, slander and harmful talk about people who are absent.

o: a believer who tells others about their own faith
someone whose words about others are true, fair and kind
someone who gives sworn testimony in a church court

s: if what you say about someone is true, it can't do harm
the Catholic catechism calls telling someone's real faults without good reason detraction: true, and harmful.
Luther read this commandment as asking more than not lying
his Small Catechism says to defend your neighbor, speak well of them and take what they do in the kindest way.
"the words of a talebearer are as wounds."

games.q: the lunch table goes quiet, and someone turns to you: is she really sick, or isn't she? what do you do?
o: share what you've heard; it's only a question.
say you don't know, and say something kind and true about her.
games.why: Luther's catechism asks for exactly that turn: not only no lie, but defend your neighbor, speak well of them, and read what they do in the kindest way.

practice: Bring to mind one person you might talk about today, a coworker, a relative, a name in the news, and notice what you'd usually say. Then try Luther's turn: find one true thing you could say in their defense, and just hold it.
If you pray, you can use an old line from Psalm 141: "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips."

wordCard.voice: Truthful witness. Someone whose words about a neighbor are true, fair and kind, whether that neighbor is in the room or not.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Exodus 20:16: a false witness, a witness of a lie.

carryVoice: Your line: speak truly. Even about someone who isn't in the room. Rest well.
